title: Smart Home Without Cloud: Local Device Communication
description: Keep your smart home private. Pilot Protocol connects devices locally with encrypted P2P - no cloud account needed. See the technical details.
seoTitle: Smart Home Without Cloud: Local Device Communication
author: Pilot Protocol editorial team

children.text: In January 2026, Belkin shut down the Wemo cloud service. Overnight, every Wemo smart plug, light switch, and motion sensor lost remote access and scheduled automations. Users who had spent hundreds of dollars on Wemo devices woke up to apps that could not connect. Some devices stopped working entirely. The community response was predictable: "Why does a light switch in my house need permission from a server in California?"

Belkin is not the first. Insteon collapsed in April 2022 with no warning. The company went dark, its cloud servers went offline, and millions of devices became unresponsive. There was no migration path. There was no transition period. One day the system worked, and the next day it did not. Google shut down its Cloud IoT Core service in August 2023, forcing every industrial and consumer IoT project built on it to find a new backend within 12 months.

The pattern is always the same: a company decides a cloud service is no longer profitable, and the hardware that depends on it becomes electronic waste. The device in your house works fine. The motor spins, the relay clicks, the sensor reads temperature. But the software that coordinates it lives on someone else's server, and when that server disappears, so does the coordination.
These are not obscure startups. These are major brands that sold millions of devices with an implicit promise: buy the hardware, and it will keep working.

-- The company ceased operations without notice. The CEO disappeared. The cloud servers went offline. Hub-dependent devices stopped responding to commands. Users with hundreds of Insteon switches and sensors had to physically rewire their homes or reverse-engineer the local protocol. A community group eventually acquired the intellectual property and began rebuilding, but the damage was done.

-- Google deprecated its IoT device management platform with a 12-month sunset timeline. Every project that used IoT Core for device provisioning, telemetry, and command delivery had to migrate to a different service. Google recommended third-party alternatives. The message was clear: Google does not consider IoT device management a core business.

-- Belkin ended cloud support for the Wemo product line. Scheduled automations stopped. Remote access stopped. The local control that some Wemo devices supported continued to work for users who knew how to find it, but the app that most people used became non-functional. Four years of product development, gone.

Each of these failures shares a root cause: the devices never talked to each other directly. They talked to a cloud service, and the cloud service coordinated everything. When the cloud disappeared, so did the coordination. The hardware was always capable of local communication. The architecture just never allowed it.

"Matter is local-first." This is the marketing message from the Connectivity Standards Alliance, backed by Apple, Google, Amazon, and Samsung. Matter devices communicate over Thread (a low-power mesh network) or Wi-Fi, using local protocols that do not require cloud connectivity for basic operation. On paper, this is exactly what the smart home community has been asking for.

In practice, the commissioning process tells a different story. When a Home Assistant user tries to add a Matter device, the system contacts Google's servers to complete the commissioning flow. A user on the Home Assistant forums described the experience: "If Matter is a supposedly local protocol, why does Home Assistant contact Google to add devices?" Another wrote: "Why does HA try to phone Google to get the OK to add a light bulb?"

The answer is that Matter uses a Distributed Compliance Ledger (DCL) -- a blockchain-based registry of certified devices -- and commissioning requires attestation that the device is genuine. In practice, this means the commissioning controller (your phone or hub) needs to verify the device's Device Attestation Certificate against a root of trust, which is managed by the CSA and distributed through infrastructure that includes cloud endpoints.

The result is a "local" protocol that requires internet access during setup. Once commissioned, the device operates locally. But the 30-minute registration process -- logging into manufacturer websites, creating accounts, linking ecosystems -- is exactly the experience that users were trying to escape. One commenter captured the frustration precisely: "30 minutes logging into somebody else's website, registering the product on their website, just to turn on a light."

Local operation after setup is not the same as local-first. A local-first system never requires cloud connectivity at any point in its lifecycle. Not during setup. Not during updates. Not during normal operation. If any step in the chain depends on an external server, you have a single point of failure you do not control.
Local-first is not a feature. It is an architecture constraint. A local-first smart home system must satisfy four properties:
You should not need to create an account on anyone's website to use hardware you own. The device works because it is plugged in, not because a database entry exists in a company's cloud.

Every function -- setup, operation, automation, remote access -- works without internet connectivity. The internet can enhance the experience (firmware updates, voice assistant integration), but the core functionality must not depend on it.

The device you bought should work indefinitely. If the manufacturer goes bankrupt, gets acquired, or decides to pivot to a different market, your hardware continues to function. There is no recurring payment that, if missed, degrades your system.

Every device needs a stable identity that survives reboots, firmware updates, network changes, and hardware replacements. When you refer to "the kitchen light," that reference should resolve to the same device today, tomorrow, and five years from now, without a DNS lookup to someone else's server.
These are not aspirational goals. They are engineering requirements. If any of them is violated, you have a system that can be bricked by someone else's business decision.

Pilot Protocol is an overlay network originally designed for AI agent communication. It provides virtual addresses, encrypted tunnels, NAT traversal, and a trust model -- all over UDP -- and its coordination servers (a registry and a beacon) are open source, so you can run them on your own hardware. The same properties that make it useful for agents make it applicable to local-first IoT.

The key difference: Pilot can run entirely on your local network. By default a daemon registers with the public backbone that Vulture Labs runs. For a smart home, run the open-source rendezvous server (registry and beacon in one process) on a hub in your house and point every device at it; then there is no external service to depend on, no account to create, and no subscription to maintain. The daemon also polls a message-of-the-day feed and sends telemetry by default; start

fields.code:
# Point a device agent (e.g., a temperature sensor) at the hub's registry and beacon
$ pilotctl init --hostname kitchen-temp --registry hub.local:9000 --beacon hub.local:9001

# Start the daemon (it creates the identity on first start)
$ pilotctl daemon start --email admin@home.local
Daemon running (pid 812)
  Address:  0:0000.0000.0002
  Hostname: kitchen-temp
  ...

children.text: The device now has a permanent 48-bit virtual address (

) and an Ed25519 cryptographic identity. That address and identity persist across reboots, firmware updates, and network changes. The address is not tied to an IP, a MAC address, or a DHCP lease. It is a logical identifier that maps to the device's current physical location on the network.
The architecture for a Pilot-based smart home is straightforward. Every device runs a lightweight Pilot daemon that handles discovery, encryption, and communication.

fields.code:
# Home network layout:
#
# Raspberry Pi (hub)      -- rendezvous server (registry + beacon), plus a daemon, addr 0:0000.0000.0001
# Kitchen temp sensor     -- pilot daemon, addr 0:0000.0000.0002
# Living room light       -- pilot daemon, addr 0:0000.0000.0003
# Thermostat controller   -- pilot daemon, addr 0:0000.0000.0004
# Door lock               -- pilot daemon, addr 0:0000.0000.0005
# Automation engine       -- pilot daemon, addr 0:0000.0000.0006
#
# All communication is local: the registry and beacon run on the hub.

children.text: The automation engine is just another agent on the network. It establishes trust with each device through the handshake protocol, subscribes to sensor events, and sends commands to actuators. Here is what the event flow looks like:
The event stream uses Pilot's built-in pub/sub on port 1002; here the hub's daemon is the broker. Topics are plain strings matched exactly, and

subscribes to every topic, which is how the automation engine receives events from every sensor type. When a threshold is crossed, it sends a command via the data exchange port (1001). All communication is encrypted end-to-end with X25519 + AES-256-GCM.
Each device runs one daemon. Measure its memory and CPU on your own hardware before packing many daemons onto one board.
Comparison: Pilot vs. Zigbee vs. Matter/Thread vs. MQTT
Yes, with a self-hosted registry and beacon

The most common reason people accept cloud dependency is remote access. "I want to check my thermostat from work." "I want to lock the front door from my phone." Fair requirements. But cloud is not the only way to satisfy them.

Pilot Protocol includes built-in NAT traversal: STUN discovers the public endpoint, UDP hole-punching establishes direct connections where possible, and the configured beacon provides ciphertext relay fallback. A phone running the daemon can reach home devices without opening router ports or deploying a VPN, but relay-backed traffic still transits that beacon.

fields.code:
# From your phone (connected to mobile data, behind carrier NAT)
$ pilotctl send-message door-lock --data '{"action": "lock"}'

# Check thermostat status: --wait prints the reply, if the thermostat's software sends one
$ pilotctl send-message thermostat-ctrl --data '{"action": "get_status"}' --wait

children.text: The connection is end-to-end encrypted. If the traffic is relayed through the beacon (because your carrier NAT is symmetric), the beacon sees only encrypted bytes. It cannot read the commands or the responses. Your home automation data never touches a third-party server in cleartext.

For this to work from outside your home network, the phone has to reach your registry and beacon. You have two options: forward the hub's TCP port 9000 and UDP port 9001, or run the rendezvous server (registry and beacon together) on a small VPS. The beacon does not store data and does not decrypt traffic; for relayed paths it forwards ciphertext.

a rendezvous server you run is not a cloud dependency. It stores registrations, not your data, needs no account, and can be moved to another machine. If it goes offline, established direct tunnels keep working; new lookups and relayed paths wait until it is back. This is fundamentally different from a cloud service that owns your device graph.
Device Setup: No Accounts, No Registration
Here is the complete setup flow for adding a new device to a Pilot-based smart home. Compare this to the typical Matter onboarding experience.

fields.code:
# On the new device (e.g., a smart plug running Linux)
curl -fsSL https://pilotprotocol.network/install.sh | sh
$ pilotctl init --hostname office-plug --registry hub.local:9000 --beacon hub.local:9001
$ pilotctl daemon start --email admin@home.local
Daemon running (pid 640)
  Address:  0:0000.0000.0007
  Hostname: office-plug
  ...

# On the automation engine -- request trust by the plug's address
$ pilotctl handshake 0:0000.0000.0007 "Home automation control"
handshake request sent to node 7

# On the new device -- approve the automation engine (node 6)
# (or start daemons with --trust-auto-approve on a registry where every node is yours)
$ pilotctl approve 6
trust established with node 6

children.text: No accounts created. No manufacturer registration. Apart from downloading the installer, no outside service is involved once the device points at your hub. The device has a permanent address, a cryptographic identity, and an encrypted connection to the automation engine. If the manufacturer goes bankrupt tomorrow, nothing changes.

In a traditional smart home, device discovery relies on protocol-specific mechanisms: Zigbee device interviews, Matter commissioning, mDNS broadcasting. Each protocol has its own discovery format, and devices from different protocols cannot discover each other without a bridge.
Pilot uses a simpler approach: give each device a function-named hostname and resolve it by name. There is no tag or capability search, so a group such as "all lights" is a list you keep yourself.

fields.code:
# Name devices by function (on each device)
$ pilotctl set-hostname living-room-light

# Resolve one device by name (it must trust you, share a network with you, or be public)
$ pilotctl find living-room-light
Hostname:  living-room-light
Node ID:   3
Address:   0:0000.0000.0003
Visible:   private

# "All lights" is your own inventory, for example a file of hostnames
$ for h in $(cat lights.txt); do pilotctl find "$h"; done

children.text: You can also attach up to three tags to a device with

(lowercase letters, digits and hyphens). The registry stores them as metadata, but nothing searches them for you. Hostnames need no schema, no ontology, and no central authority defining what "light" means. The convention is up to you. This is less structured than a formal device model, but it is also less brittle. When a new device type appears that did not exist when the standard was written, you just pick a new name.

Pilot Protocol is not a device protocol. It needs to be said clearly because the comparison table above might suggest it is a drop-in replacement for Zigbee or Thread. It is not. Here are the real limitations:

Pilot runs over IP networks (Wi-Fi or Ethernet). It cannot talk to Zigbee radios, Z-Wave chips, or Thread border routers directly. Devices need to be IP-capable. For battery-powered sensors that use Zigbee or Thread for power efficiency, you still need a Zigbee coordinator or Thread border router. Pilot can coordinate the coordinators, but it does not replace the radio layer.

Pilot does not know how to dim a light or read a temperature sensor. It provides the communication channel. The application logic that translates "set brightness to 50%" into the correct GPIO command lives in the device firmware, not in Pilot.

There is no phone app with a nice dashboard showing your rooms and devices. The Pilot CLI shows node status, but it is designed for agent fleet management, not home automation. A consumer-friendly UI would need to be built on top.
Needs a computer, not a microcontroller.

The Pilot daemon and CLI are static Go binaries. This works on Raspberry Pi, Intel NUCs, and any Linux SBC. It does not run on microcontrollers (ESP32, Arduino) without significant porting effort. For microcontroller-based devices, you would need a bridge device running the Pilot daemon that translates between the microcontroller's native protocol and the Pilot network.

There are no Home Assistant plugins, no Alexa skills, no Google Home actions. Pilot is a communication layer, not a home automation platform. Integration with existing platforms would require custom development.

Pilot's value proposition for smart home is narrow but specific: with a self-hosted registry and beacon, it is a coordination layer that does not depend on anyone else's infrastructure. If you are building a custom home automation system from IP-capable devices and you want it to survive any vendor's business decisions, Pilot provides the addressing, encryption, discovery, and remote access. The device control, automation logic, and user interface are your responsibility.
When the Next Cloud Shuts Down

It will happen again. A company will decide that maintaining a cloud service for smart home devices is not worth the cost. The devices will stop working. Users will be angry. Forum posts will be written. And then it will happen again.

The only defense is architectural. If your devices talk to each other through infrastructure you own and operate, no business decision by anyone else can break your home. The hub in your closet does not care about quarterly earnings calls. The virtual addresses assigned to your devices are permanent. There is no subscription model. There is no service that can be discontinued.

This is not a new idea. The internet itself was designed to be decentralized and resilient. Somewhere along the way, convenience centralized everything. The path back is not through better cloud services. It is through architecture that does not need them.
